summary: Analyzes what a routing protocol needs to do in industrial plants that use low-power, lossy wireless networks of field devices such as sensors and actuators. It lists functional requirements around reliability, latency, and security. It is an informational requirements document, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Industrial plants use wireless field devices to collect measurements and control equipment, but their links and power supplies can be limited. RFC 5673 describes what an IPv6 routing protocol for these low-power and lossy networks should support.

subtitle: Routing requirements for industrial field devices using low-power and lossy networks.

tldr.problem: Industrial wireless field devices use constrained, unreliable links, while the RFC notes that open routing standards for LLNs were lacking.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes industrial traffic, topology, and device limits, then lists requirements for routing by service needs, reliability, device resources, mobility, manageability, and security.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5673 is a requirements document, not a routing protocol. It provides input for routing work on industrial low-power and lossy networks.

facts.label: Convergence after joining
facts.value: MUST within several minutes; SHOULD within tens of seconds

today: RFC 5673 is Informational and was published in October 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document defines requirements, not a protocol.

sections.title: Why Industrial LLNs Need Routing Requirements
sections.content:
Industrial networks are adding wireless field devices alongside existing wired systems. The RFC describes IPv6 as a technology used by industrial wireless specifications, but notes that those specifications left routing to proprietary methods because open LLN routing standards were lacking.

This document analyzes requirements for an IPv6 routing protocol in industrial low-power and lossy networks. It is not a protocol specification. The RFC uses MUST, SHOULD, and MAY with the meanings defined by RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes what routing must support for industrial wireless field devices. It lists requirements rather than specifying the routing protocol itself.

sections.title: Applications and Traffic Patterns
sections.content:
Industrial process applications are grouped into six classes: emergency safety action; three forms of control; alerting; and logging or data transfer. Time-critical delivery matters more as the class number decreases. For control applications, variation in delay can matter as much as delay itself.

Most near-term LLN traffic is low-frequency data collection. The RFC says 90% of the market is covered by packet rates between one per second and one per hour, with an average below one per minute. Alarms and bursty reports may need lower latency, while bulk transfers need temporary resources for a transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Many industrial devices report measurements periodically, while alarms need faster delivery. Different traffic types have different requirements for delay, reliability, and bandwidth.

sections.title: Topology and Device Constraints
sections.content:
The RFC says most existing applications can be served by networks of 10 to 200 field devices with at most 20 hops. Field devices may route traffic, and their routing roles can change over time to share forwarding costs. A backbone can connect several smaller wireless networks.

Devices use batteries, energy scavenging, or line power and have limited memory and processing. The network may carry different logical topologies for different applications, even when those applications share the radio medium. The RFC emphasizes separating LLNs from other plant and office network domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Industrial LLNs may be small meshes or several networks connected by a backbone. Devices have different power and memory limits, so route choices need to account for those differences.

sections.title: Routing, Reliability, and Operations
sections.content:
Routing must support different link metrics and compute constrained, potentially unidirectional routes for different flows. It must allow multiple paths to the same destination and account for node constraints such as battery energy and memory. Multicast should be supported. After a device joins, the protocol must converge within several minutes and should do so within tens of seconds.

The protocol should support walking users and vehicles moving at up to 35 kmph. Installation should require little specialized effort, with automated authentication and configuration. The RFC recognizes tradeoffs between power use, security, ease of setup, and convergence as networks grow.
sections.plainLanguage: Routes should reflect each flow's needs and the resources of the nodes carrying it. The protocol should adapt when links or devices change without making setup difficult.

sections.title: Security in Industrial Environments
sections.content:
The RFC treats security as important because industrial systems can have financial and human-safety consequences. Field devices may have limited physical protection and could be compromised. The routing protocol should limit the impact of a compromised node and use secure messages for configuration and management.

New devices must authenticate before joining self-configuration, and wireless access points must preserve separation between the LLN and connected plant domains. The document leaves detailed implications for a routing protocol to future work.
sections.plainLanguage: New devices should prove their identity before joining routing. A compromised field device should not be able to disrupt the whole network.
